blocks.text: Given a non negative integer num, convert it into its English words representation, exactly the way it would be read aloud.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Long Number Aloud in Chunks
blocks.text: This is exactly how a long number is read aloud, broken into chunks of three digits at a time, from the largest chunk down to the smallest, announcing "thousand", "million", or "billion" after each chunk that needs it. The way any single chunk of three digits is read never changes, whether it happens to be the billions chunk or the very last one.

blocks.caption: Split the number into groups of three digits, convert each the same way, and attach a scale word

blocks.text: 12345 is "Twelve Thousand Three Hundred Forty Five".
Zero is simply "Zero", its own special case.
Unlike most problems on this sheet, it is worth first asking whether there is even an asymptotic complexity to chase here at all.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The input is always at most ten digits long, so there is no growing input size here, and therefore no complexity class to improve, every version of this solution already runs in constant time.

Observation 2: The real problem with a first attempt is not speed, it is that the exact same three digit group conversion rule, hundred, ten, one, ends up written out four separate times, once for billions, once for millions, once for thousands, and once for the final group, a maintenance and correctness risk rather than a performance one.

Observation 3: Testing this against num equal to 12345 confirms it, whichever group is being converted, thousands or the final group, the exact same hundred-ten-one rule applies, only the group's value and its scale word differ.

Observation 4: Since the conversion rule itself never depends on which group is being converted, it can be extracted into a single reusable helper, called once per non zero group, replacing four duplicated blocks with one that only ever needs to be tested a single time.
That reframing, this is a code duplication problem wearing a math problem's clothing, is what turns "optimize this" from a speed question into a maintainability one.

Split the number directly into its billions, millions, thousands, and final three digit group. Then convert each of those four groups into words using its own separately written block of hundred, ten, and one digit logic.

items: If the number is zero, return "Zero" immediately.
Extract the billions, millions, thousands, and final group using division and modulo.
For each of the four groups, if it is non zero, convert it to words using an inline block of logic, and append the group's scale word if it has one.
Join every non empty piece together with spaces.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: convert each of the four fixed groups using its own separate inline logic

codes.python:
ONES = ["", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten",
        "Eleven", "Twelve", "Thirteen", "Fourteen", "Fifteen", "Sixteen", "Seventeen", "Eighteen", "Nineteen"]
TENS = ["", "", "Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty", "Sixty", "Seventy", "Eighty", "Ninety"]

def number_to_words(num):
    if num == 0:
        return "Zero"
    billions = num // 1_000_000_000
    millions = (num // 1_000_000) % 1000
    thousands = (num // 1000) % 1000
    ones_group = num % 1000
    words = []

    if billions > 0:                              # convert the billions group, inline
        wb = []
        if billions >= 100:
            wb.append(ONES[billions // 100]); wb.append("Hundred"); billions %= 100
        if billions >= 20:
            wb.append(TENS[billions // 10]); billions %= 10
        if billions > 0:
            wb.append(ONES[billions])
        words.append(" ".join(wb))
        words.append("Billion")

    if millions > 0:                              # convert the millions group, inline, same logic repeated
        wm = []
        if millions >= 100:
            wm.append(ONES[millions // 100]); wm.append("Hundred"); millions %= 100
        if millions >= 20:
            wm.append(TENS[millions // 10]); millions %= 10
        if millions > 0:
            wm.append(ONES[millions])
        words.append(" ".join(wm))
        words.append("Million")

    if thousands > 0:                             # convert the thousands group, inline, same logic again
        wt = []
        if thousands >= 100:
            wt.append(ONES[thousands // 100]); wt.append("Hundred"); thousands %= 100
        if thousands >= 20:
            wt.append(TENS[thousands // 10]); thousands %= 10
        if thousands > 0:
            wt.append(ONES[thousands])
        words.append(" ".join(wt))
        words.append("Thousand")

    if ones_group > 0:                            # convert the final group, inline, same logic a fourth time
        wo = []
        if ones_group >= 100:
            wo.append(ONES[ones_group // 100]); wo.append("Hundred"); ones_group %= 100
        if ones_group >= 20:
            wo.append(TENS[ones_group // 10]); ones_group %= 10
        if ones_group > 0:
            wo.append(ONES[ones_group])
        words.append(" ".join(wo))

    return " ".join(words)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num = 12345
    print(number_to_words(num))

blocks.text: This is correct, since every one of the four possible groups is genuinely converted using the same hundred, ten, and one digit rules, just written out separately each time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), since the number of digits is always bounded by a small constant, there is no growing input size here to speak of.
Space: O(1) beyond the output string. This problem is not really about asymptotic complexity, since the input size never grows, it is about how the solution is structured.

Limitation: the exact same hundred, ten, and one digit conversion logic is written out four separate times, once for each group. That is a real maintenance risk, a bug fixed in one copy could easily be forgotten in the other three. Since every group is converted using identical rules, that logic only needs to be written once, as a single reusable helper called for every group in turn.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the four inline blocks work but are risky: they are copy pasted from each other, so any future bug fix or edge case correction has to be remembered and applied in all four places, not just one.

What is genuinely different about the "optimization" here compared to most problems on this sheet: there is no speed to gain, the number of operations is already bounded by a small constant, the improvement is entirely about reducing duplicated logic.

What stays true across every group: the exact same hundred-ten-one conversion rule applies no matter which group, billions, millions, thousands, or the final group, is being converted.

Can that rule be factored out completely: yes, a single helper that converts any value from 0 to 999 into words handles every group identically, with only the group's own value and scale word varying from call to call.

The core idea: write the three digit conversion rule exactly once, as a reusable helper, then peel the number into groups of three digits and call that one helper for each non zero group.

Write one helper function that converts any number from 0 to 999 into words. Then repeatedly peel off the last three digits of the input, call that single helper on each group, and attach the appropriate scale word, "Thousand", "Million", or "Billion", based on that group's position.
Peel the number into groups of three digits, and call one shared helper on every non zero group, attaching the correct scale word based on that group's position.

blocks.text: Joining these together in order gives "Twelve Thousand Three Hundred Forty Five", the same result as before, using a single reusable helper instead of four separate copies.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: peel off one group at a time and send every group through the same helper

blocks.text: This works because the three digit conversion rule is a pure function of the group's own value alone, it never depends on which position that group occupies; the position only ever affects which scale word gets appended afterward. Separating "how to convert a group" from "which scale word this group needs" means one correctly written and tested helper can safely serve every group, no matter how many of them there are.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), the same order as the brute force, since the number of digits is still bounded by a constant.
Space: O(1) beyond the output string. The real improvement here is not in speed, it is that one well tested helper function replaces four duplicated blocks of logic, removing an entire category of copy paste mistakes.

blocks.text: Not every problem is about finding a faster algorithm, some are about recognizing that the same piece of logic is being repeated and factoring it out into one place. This problem is a clean example of that, the billions, millions, thousands, and final groups are all converted by the exact same rule, and writing that rule once is both shorter and safer than writing it four times.

items: Forgetting that a group is only converted, and its scale word only attached, when that group is non zero, otherwise phrases like "Zero Thousand" would incorrectly appear.
Getting the boundary between the tens words and the teen words wrong, values from ten through nineteen have their own irregular names rather than following the usual tens plus ones pattern.
Leaving extra spaces in the final result when a group contributes no words at all.

blocks.text: Pointing out early that this problem has no real asymptotic complexity to optimize, since the input size never grows, and that the real skill being tested is recognizing repeated logic and factoring it into a single helper, shows a clear understanding of what this problem is actually asking.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you make this faster", think: there is no growing input here, the number of digits is already bounded by a constant, so speed is not the axis to improve.
If the interviewer says "can you clean this up", think: the four group conversions are identical logic, extract one reusable helper.
If the interviewer says "what about the teens", think: ten through nineteen are irregular names, they must be listed explicitly rather than derived from a tens-plus-ones formula.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(1) time and O(1) space beyond the output, since the number of digits is always bounded by a small constant. The real difference is not speed, it is that the optimized version replaces four duplicated blocks of conversion logic with a single reusable helper function, reused for every group.

items: Pattern: duplicated logic extraction, recognizing that four separately written blocks of conversion logic are actually the exact same rule, and factoring it into a single reusable helper.

Core Idea: the hundred-ten-one conversion rule is identical for every group regardless of its position, so it can be written once as a shared helper and called for every non zero group, with only the scale word varying by position.
Time: O(1) for both versions, since the input is always bounded by a small, fixed number of digits.
Space: O(1) beyond the output string for both versions.
Most Important Observation: not every "optimize this" question is about speed, some are about recognizing and removing duplicated logic to reduce maintenance risk.

Interview Difficulty: easy to produce a correct but duplicated brute force; explicitly naming that this is a code quality improvement, not a speed one, and then factoring out the shared helper is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: one helper converts any group from 0 to 999 the same way, only the scale word depends on position.
